operation_tail.detail: Ofcom states that every UK home and business has the legal right to request a decent, affordable broadband connection, subject to the USO eligibility rules.
A USO decent connection requires a download speed of at least 10 Mbit/s; lower estimates do not satisfy the threshold.
A USO decent connection also requires an upload speed of at least 1 Mbit/s; the download threshold alone is insufficient.
USO requests are handled by BT across the UK or KCOM in the Hull area; provider designation is geographic and not inferred from the retail ISP.
An applicant does not need to be an existing BT or KCOM customer to request a USO eligibility assessment.
An existing fixed-wireless or satellite service may provide a faster connection and can affect whether a premise lacks access to decent broadband.
BT or KCOM have 30 days after contact to confirm eligibility and the estimated cost of building the connection.
Eligibility requires that the home or business has no access to an existing service meeting the decent-broadband standard.
A premise is not eligible where a UK or devolved-government public broadband scheme is expected to cover it within the next 12 months.
A premise with access only to a decent service priced above £59.60 per month may still request a universal-service connection.
Where the applicant's share of network construction or upgrade cost is £3,400 or less, the applicant does not pay for that build work.
If the connection cost exceeds £3,400, the applicant may proceed by paying the excess above the threshold.
For an excess-cost connection, BT or KCOM conduct a survey and provide a quote within 60 days.
A completed USO connection is charged at the same retail price as the same package supplied to other customers.
The new USO broadband service is capped at no more than £59.60 per month under the current Ofcom consumer guidance.
Ofcom states that most eligible applicants should receive the connection within 12 months.
Some USO builds may take up to 24 months, so the connection timetable is not treated as immediate availability.
Where a premise is not eligible, satellite broadband may be offered as an alternative and requires installation of a dish.
BT or KCOM must explain an applicant's right to challenge an adverse eligibility decision and how to complain.
Customers have free access to alternative dispute resolution for unresolved USO eligibility complaints.
Alternative dispute resolution becomes available after eight weeks without resolution or earlier when deadlock is reached.
A person does not need to be an existing BT or KCOM customer to dispute an eligibility decision.
Ofcom uses complaint evidence for regulatory oversight but does not investigate or resolve individual USO complaints.
The Ofcom social-tariff guidance and provider table are bound to the page's 22 June 2026 update date.
Social tariffs are discounted broadband or phone packages for people receiving Universal Credit, Pension Credit and certain other benefits.
Social tariffs are delivered in the same way as ordinary packages; the distinction is price and eligibility rather than a separate coverage technology.
Ofcom's current listed social-tariff prices range from £10 to £24 per month and are treated as time-sensitive provider offers.
Ofcom characterises the listed fixed social tariffs as fast, unlimited broadband, but this consumer description is not a premise-coverage measurement.
Most listed social broadband tariffs offer speeds above 30 Mbit/s, while individual package speeds remain provider-specific.
Setup is normally free or low-cost, and any charge should be disclosed before signup.
Where an existing provider offers a social tariff, an eligible customer can switch to it at any time without a switching charge.
Ofcom states that the agreed social-tariff price will not rise during the contract.
Customers can leave a social tariff before its contractual end without paying an exit fee.
If the customer or someone in the household receives Universal Credit, the household can apply for the listed tariffs subject to provider checks.
Ofcom says all major providers also include Pension Credit, Employment and Support Allowance, Jobseeker's Allowance and Income Support.
Some providers extend eligibility to additional benefits such as Personal Independence Payment or Attendance Allowance.
The person receiving the qualifying benefit generally needs to be the main person named on the service contract.
Most social tariffs can be requested online or by calling the provider to switch.
When the current provider has no social tariff, the customer may switch to a provider that offers one.
Ofcom notes that a provider may permit an eligible customer to leave an existing contract without a penalty; this is not guaranteed for every provider.
A provider listed for a country or region may not cover every premise in that area.
Actual service availability must be checked with the provider or Ofcom coverage checker rather than inferred from the social-tariff table.
The Ofcom table includes both fixed-broadband tariffs and mobile or 5G offers; these service types are not merged into one fixed-coverage field.
Package names, prices, advertised speeds and geographic scopes are provider-controlled and must be refreshed rather than treated as permanent data.
If all submitted deployments are realised, full fibre could reach 28.1 million UK homes by January 2029.
The 28.1 million full-fibre projection corresponds to 92% of UK residential properties.
The projection starts from the January 2026 existing-coverage baseline of 24.9 million homes, or 82%.
All submitted plans could raise gigabit-capable coverage to 29 million homes, or 95%, by January 2029.
The gigabit projection is compared with the January 2026 baseline of 27.1 million homes, or 89%.
The new all-plans full-fibre projection for January 2028 is 90%, below the 95% projection reported from the previous year's plans.
Using High Confidence plans only, January 2028 full-fibre coverage could be 87%, compared with 86% under the previous plan vintage.
High Confidence full-fibre plans could produce 88% residential coverage by January 2029.
Under all plans, January 2029 projections for England, Scotland and Wales are one to two percentage points lower than the previous year's January 2028 projections.
Northern Ireland's all-plans full-fibre projection remains at 99% in the reported comparison.
Urban residential gigabit coverage could rise from 24.2 million homes, or 93%, to 25.3 million, or 97%, by January 2029.
Rural residential gigabit coverage could rise from 2.9 million homes, or 66%, to 3.7 million, or 86%, by January 2029.
Ofcom reports submitted network build plans affecting every local authority.
If all plans are realised, 95% of local authorities are estimated to reach at least 85% residential gigabit-capable coverage by January 2029.
Some deployment plans add first coverage while others overbuild existing networks or other planned networks; planned records are not unique uncovered premises.
By the end of 2028, 73% of UK homes, or 22.2 million, could access at least two gigabit-capable networks.
By the end of 2028, 36% of UK homes, or 11.1 million, could access at least three gigabit-capable networks.
Around 6,950 geographically distinct FWA masts are planned or scheduled for upgrade between January 2026 and January 2029.
The planned FWA expansion concerns networks intended to offer high-speed broadband of at least 100 Mbit/s download.
The PND2026 headline findings refer to residential properties; all-premises results are supplied separately for local authorities.
Sixty-five official USO, social-tariff, affordability and planned-deployment controls were published line by line while exact Ofcom r2 coverage promotions remained fail-closed.
